## Further Reading

American Institute of Certified Public Accountants. (2026). *Guide to audit data analytics*. <https://www.aicpa-cima.com/cpe-learning/publication/guide-to-audit-data-analytics> The AICPA's guide to the use of data analytics in audits. It includes practical considerations for assessing the reliability of the data that an analytic uses, the question behind every population check in this chapter.

Drake, P. D., & Nigrini, M. J. (2000). Computer assisted analytical procedures using Benford's Law. *Journal of Accounting Education*, *18*(2), 127–146. <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0748-5751(00)00008-7> A teaching case in which you analyze a real accounts payable file with digit tests as an analytical procedure in an external audit, then graph and report the results. It applies three digit tests where Tutorial 8.1 applies one.

Fay, R. G., & Negangard, E. M. (2017). Manual journal entry testing: Data analytics and the risk of fraud. *Journal of Accounting Education*, *38*, 37–49. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaccedu.2016.12.004> A teaching case in two phases: validating that a file of manual journal entries is complete, and then testing the entries for red flags of fraud, such as who recorded them, when they were created, their descriptions, and whether they were back-posted. It parallels Tutorial 8.3 with audit software instead of Excel.

Nigrini, M. J. (2012). *Benford's Law: Applications for forensic accounting, auditing, and fraud detection*. Wiley. <https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119203094> A book-length treatment of digit analysis in forensic accounting and auditing, and the source of the conformity ranges for the mean absolute deviation used in this chapter.

Nigrini, M. J. (2017). Audit sampling using Benford's Law: A review of the literature with some new perspectives. *Journal of Emerging Technologies in Accounting*, *14*(2), 29–46. <https://doi.org/10.2308/jeta-51783> A review of the accounting applications of Benford's Law that examines a proposed Benford-based sampling method, finds that it can produce large samples of questionable accuracy, and discusses which audit data are appropriate for digit analysis.

Nigrini, M. J. (2019). The patterns of the numbers used in occupational fraud schemes. *Managerial Auditing Journal*, *34*(5), 606–626. <https://doi.org/10.1108/MAJ-11-2017-1717> A classification of the numbers found in fraud cases: round amounts, amounts just above or below control thresholds, duplicates of authentic transactions, and outliers, among others. It connects each pattern to tests like those of this chapter and discusses how to deal with false positives.

Public Company Accounting Oversight Board. (n.d.-e). *AS 2401: Consideration of fraud in a financial statement audit*. <https://pcaobus.org/oversight/standards/auditing-standards/details/AS2401> The auditing standard on fraud for audits of public companies. Its paragraphs on journal entries explain why auditors test them, the characteristics of fraudulent entries, and when testing should focus on the end of the period.
